doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Church community, living in the parsonage, grandfather's death
summary: Close-knit church-centred black community, living in the parsonage, grandfather's death, early lack of awareness of racism, Sunday church routine.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Was the black community a close-knit community?
Close, yes.
It was? So, you knew basically everyone?
It was based around the church, as usual.
And your grandfather was…?
He was a minister. We moved out there because he had been assigned to a church there.
And where did you live?
We lived in the parsonage. The parsonage is always next door to the church. We lived there until he died. After we had been out there for three or four years, he died.
If you left when you were four, it was when you were seven or eight?
Yes, right.
So, essentially, the head of the household became your grandmother?
Yes, my grandmother.
Did this have an adverse impact on your livelihood at that point?

I don’t know. No, because I was still very young. When he died, I was like six or seven, less than ten years old anyway, so I wasn’t doing anything but getting up and going to school. So, it had no effect at all.
Do you remember suffering any of the indignation of segregated society or racism at an early age?

At that early an age, no. I just remembered somehow you get this knowledge that you’re not supposed to do this, you’re not supposed to do that, and whatever people tell you at that age, there’s a tendency just to ask why, maybe, but you’ll just accept it or something. It didn’t have any real impact on me until I got older.
What part of town was the so-called black section of town? Where were you located? North, east, south, west?

There were two parts. The city was separated by a street called Central Avenue, so the east of Central Avenue was the east side, and west was the west side. At one time, when we first lived there, we lived on the west side, and then we lived on the east side. It was a pretty close-knit community of people, like I said, based around the church mostly.
The church figured very largely in your young life?
Yes, very largely. We used to go to church on Sunday like two, three times a day.
Whoa.
I had to go to Sunday school in the morning and then the regular church at 11 o’clock, and then the evening church at 6 o’clock.
How about Wednesday night prayer meeting?
No, we didn’t have to do that one.
What was the denomination? Was it AME?
AME, yeah.
